In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: Discovering Bias in Latent Space: An Unsupervised Debiasing Approach
papers.research_question: Can we mitigate bias directly in the model representation space and do so without labeled data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STEER FAIR, an unsupervised inference-time activation steering algorithm that identifies bias directions in a model's representation space and steers activations away from them to mitigate bias, particularly option ordering bias in question-answering.
papers.conclusion: Introduces STEER FAIR, an approach for unsupervised mitigation of bias in question-answering models operating directly in the model representation space, which improves performance across benchmark tasks and matches supervised baselines.
papers.key_findings:
STEER FAIR significantly reduces instruction-tuned model performance variance across prompt modifications on three benchmark tasks.
The unsupervised method surpasses a supervised baseline (ITI) with 100 labels and matches performance with 500 labels.
The identified bias direction is generalizable across datasets with the same task.
Only a small number of unlabeled sample demonstrations are sufficient to identify effective bias directions.
Steering bias directions does not negatively impact base model performance.
papers.limitation:
The accurate identification of bias directions depends on the existence of directions in activation space that effectively summarize bias, requiring separation between usable knowledge and bias. The precise circumstances under which these conditions hold remain unclear.
Absence of theoretical characterizations for hyperparameters and the required number of unlabeled samples.
future_direction: Extension of the method to accommodate non-enumerable bias, such as exploring latent directions associated with harmful text generation or misinformation.
papers.abstract: The question-answering (QA) capabilities of foundation models are highly sensitive to prompt variations, rendering their performance susceptible to superficial, non-meaning-altering changes. This vulnerability often stems from the model's preference or bias towards specific input characteristics, such as option position or superficial image features in multi-modal settings. We propose to rectify this bias directly in the model's internal representation. Our approach, SteerFair, finds the bias direction in the model's representation space and steers activation values away from it during inference. Specifically, we exploit the observation that bias often adheres to simple association rules, such as the spurious association between the first option and correctness likelihood. Next, we construct demonstrations of these rules from unlabeled samples and use them to identify the bias directions. We empirically show that SteerFair significantly reduces instruction-tuned model performance variance across prompt modifications on three benchmark tasks. Remarkably, our approach surpasses a supervised baseline with 100 labels by an average of 10.86% accuracy points and 12.95 score points and matches the performance with 500 labels.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: The Queen of England is not England's Queen: On the Lack of Factual Coherency in PLMs
papers.research_question: What is the coherency of factual knowledge in Pre-trained Language Models, and how does it vary with different prompts and evidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of coherency for factual knowledge in PLMs, demonstrates that PLMs have low coherency, and finds that including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
papers.conclusion: PLMs have poor coherency in factual knowledge, but evidence paragraphs help. Future work should focus on architectural, data, and interface improvements.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs have low coherency in factual knowledge.
Autoregressive PLMs perform worse than masked PLMs.
Optimized prompts do not improve coherency.
Including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
Coherency varies significantly with paraphrased prompts.
papers.limitation: For N-1 or N-M relations, it is difficult to exclude every possible answer, and only answers present in LAMA are excluded, which might negatively affect the results.
future_direction: Improve PLMs on architectural level.
Improve PLMs on data level.
Improve pre-training objectives and interface.
papers.abstract: Factual knowledge encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) enriches their representations and justifies their use as knowledge bases. Previous work has focused on probing PLMs for factual knowledge by measuring how often they can correctly predict an object entity given a subject and a relation, and improving fact retrieval by optimizing the prompts used for querying PLMs. In this work, we consider a complementary aspect, namely the coherency of factual knowledge in PLMs, i.e., how often can PLMs predict the subject entity given its initial prediction of the object entity. This goes beyond evaluating how much PLMs know, and focuses on the internal state of knowledge inside them. Our results indicate that PLMs have low coherency using manually written, optimized and paraphrased prompts, but including an evidence paragraph leads to substantial improvement. This shows that PLMs fail to model inverse relations and need further enhancements to be able to handle retrieving facts from their parameters in a coherent manner, and to be considered as knowledge bases.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Absolute Position Embedding Learns Sinusoid-like Waves for Attention Based on Relative Position
papers.research_question: How does the concentration of attention on nearby tokens emerge in Transformer-based models with learnable absolute position embeddings? The paper analyzes the mechanism behind this phenomenon.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that learnable absolute position embeddings acquire sinusoid-like components through pre-training, and attention heads extract these components and shift their phases to achieve concentration of attention on nearby tokens based on relative position.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzed the concentration of attention based on relative position in self-attention with learnable absolute position embedding, showing it is due to relative phase shifts of periodic components in query and key derived from position embeddings, explaining in part how absolute position embedding allows inference based on relative position.
papers.key_findings:
Learned absolute position embeddings have sinusoid-like waves with several limited frequencies.
Attention heads extract these periodic components from hidden states, as revealed by Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).
The self-attention shifts the phase of the periodic components in query and key, determining the direction of attention.
The phase shift width is constant across different frequencies, due to properties of the rotation matrix relating query and key.
For attention strongly concentrated on adjacent tokens, word embeddings also play a role.
papers.limitation:
The positional representation of GPT-2 differs significantly from encoder models, so the interpretation may not apply to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on dependence on nearby tokens, so it is unclear if position embedding helps determine which of distant tokens precedes the other.
The analysis decomposes attention scores before softmax; the non-linearity of softmax should be considered when analyzing contributions to downstream components.
future_direction: Clarify whether the phenomenon occurs in causal models (decoder-only) with symmetric self-attention.
papers.abstract: Attention weight is a clue to interpret how a Transformer-based model makes an inference. In some attention heads, the attention focuses on the neighbors of each token. This allows the output vector of each token to depend on the surrounding tokens and contributes to make the inference context-dependent. We analyze the mechanism behind the concentration of attention on nearby tokens. We show that the phenomenon emerges as follows: (1) learned position embedding has sinusoid-like components, (2) such components are transmitted to the query and the key in the self-attention, (3) the attention head shifts the phases of the sinusoid-like components so that the attention concentrates on nearby tokens at specific relative positions. In other words, a certain type of Transformer-based model acquires the sinusoidal positional encoding to some extent on its own through Masked Language Modeling.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Position Bias in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do attention masks and positional encodings shape position bias in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a graph-theoretic framework for analyzing position bias in transformers, revealing that causal masking biases attention toward earlier positions and that relative positional encodings introduce a trade-off between decay effects and cumulative importance of early positions.
papers.conclusion: Our work provides a probabilistic and graph-theoretic framework for understanding position bias in transformers, revealing the inherent bias of causal masks toward earlier tokens and the nuanced interplay with relative positional encodings, offering a foundation for designing attention mechanisms with predictable positional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Causal masking inherently biases attention toward earlier positions in deep networks, as tokens in deeper layers attend to increasingly more contextualized representations of earlier tokens.
The interaction between causal masking and relative positional encodings (e.g., decay mask, RoPE) leads to a trade-off: while they introduce distance-based decay within individual layers, their aggregate effect across layers results in non-monotonic behavior, balancing local decay and cumulative importance of early positions.
Attention sinks emerge as center nodes in the graph defined by the attention mask, explaining why they appear at certain positions (e.g., first token for causal mask, prefix tokens for prefix mask).
The causal mask does not simulate positional encodings but instead introduces a bias toward earlier positions via iterative attention, capturing positional bias only when it aligns with this predisposition.
Residual connections can modulate the accumulation of positional effects across layers, making the relationship between depth and bias non-monotonic.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not extend to other transformer components such as residual connections, value projections, and MLPs, which may interact with attention in nontrivial ways.
future_direction: Leveraging insights to design bias-free transformers, mitigating positional biases to improve model robustness and generalization.
Informing the strategic exploitation of positional bias in specific applications, such as text summarization or recommendation systems.
Extending the analysis to other transformer components, such as residual connections, value projections, and MLPs.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed various manifestations of position bias in transformer architectures, from the "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon to attention sinks, yet a comprehensive theoretical understanding of how attention masks and positional encodings shape these biases remains elusive. This paper presents a graph-theoretic framework for analyzing position bias in multi-layer attention. Modeling attention masks as directed graphs, we quantify how tokens interact with contextual information based on their sequential positions. We uncover two key insights: First, causal masking inherently biases attention toward earlier positions, as tokens in deeper layers attend to increasingly more contextualized representations of earlier tokens. Second, we characterize the competing effects of the causal mask and relative positional encodings, such as the decay mask and rotary positional encoding (RoPE): while both mechanisms introduce distance-based decay within individual attention maps, their aggregate effect across multiple attention layers$\unicode{x2013}$coupled with the causal mask$\unicode{x2013}$leads to a trade-off between the long-term decay effects and the cumulative importance of early sequence positions. Through controlled numerical experiments, we not only validate our theoretical findings but also reproduce position biases observed in real-world LLMs. Our framework offers a principled foundation for understanding positional biases in transformers, shedding light on the complex interplay of attention mechanism components and guiding more informed architectural design.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Debiasing Pretrained Text Encoders by Paying Attention to Paying Attention
papers.research_question: How can we debias pretrained text encoders by reducing bias in the attention mechanism, and does this approach reduce bias in representations and predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces AttenD, a debiasing method that reduces social stereotypes in pretrained text encoders by equalizing attention scores on social groups, thereby mitigating bias in representations and predictions with minimal semantic damage.
papers.conclusion: Attention is a key component where bias is encoded in text encoders, and reducing bias from attention effectively mitigates it from the model as a whole.
papers.key_findings:
Stereotypes are encoded in the attention layer of transformer-based text encoders.
Existing debiasing methods that operate on embeddings do not effectively reduce bias in the attention mechanism.
The proposed AttenD method successfully reduces bias in attention, which in turn reduces bias in text representations and downstream predictions.
AttenD preserves the semantic performance of the original text encoder, as shown by minimal degradation on GLUE tasks.
The method is effective across multiple text encoders (BERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, etc.) and multiple bias types (gender, race, religion).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to binary gender, race, and religion, and do not include other demographics like nationality, age, or disability.
Bias detection experiments have positive predictive ability; they can detect the presence of bias but not its absence.
Finetuning on the News-commentary-v15 corpus might introduce new biases encoded in the data.
Bias is reduced but not completely mitigated; models are not perfect after debiasing.
future_direction: Include more bias types and social groups (e.g., nationality, age, disability) in debiasing.
Incorporate human evaluation to assess stereotypical propensities of text encoders.
Produce more inclusive benchmarks for bias evaluation.
papers.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) models are found to exhibit discriminatory stereotypes across many social constructs, e.g. gender and race. In comparison to the progress made in reducing bias from static word embeddings, fairness in sentence-level text encoders received little consideration despite their wider applicability in contemporary NLP tasks. In this paper, we propose a debiasing method for pre-trained text encoders that both reduces social stereotypes, and inflicts next to no semantic damage. Unlike previous studies that directly manipulate the embeddings, we suggest to dive deeper into the operation of these encoders, and pay more attention to the way they pay attention to different social groups. We find that stereotypes are also encoded in the attention layer. Then, we work on model debiasing by redistributing the attention scores of a text encoder such that it forgets any preference to historically advantaged groups, and attends to all social classes with the same intensity. Our experiments confirm that reducing bias from attention effectively mitigates it from the model’s text representations.

papers.title: Bias A-head? Analyzing Bias in Transformer-Based Language Model Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How does bias manifest and behave internally in a language model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework to identify biased attention heads in transformer-based language models and shows that biases are encoded in a small set of heads, which can be targeted for debiasing.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that biases in language models are encoded in a small set of attention heads, and the proposed framework helps understand and mitigate these biases, contributing to more transparent and fair NLP systems.
papers.key_findings:
Biased attention heads can be identified via gradient-based bias scores, and counter-stereotype experiments validate that these heads encode stereotypes.
The distribution of biased heads differs across models, with GPT-2 having fewer biased heads than BERT.
Masking out a small set of biased heads can reduce model bias with minimal impact on language modeling and NLU performance.
LLaMA-2-Chat exhibits less bias than LLaMA-2, suggesting that RLHF reduces stereotyping.
Prior debiasing strategies may cover up bias rather than remove it, as some anti-bias heads are turned into biased heads after debiasing.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on stereotyping bias (representational harm) and not allocational bias.
Relies on existing word lists which may have limited coverage for other protected groups and non-English languages.
Focuses on attention heads only, while bias may also manifest in other model components.
Does not investigate heads with negative bias scores (anti-bias heads) in detail.
future_direction: Apply the method to assess biases in larger foundation models like GPT-3 and LLaMA.
Study allocational bias in downstream NLP tasks.
Investigate other model components and anti-bias heads for a more comprehensive understanding.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based pretrained large language models (PLM) such as BERT and GPT have achieved remarkable success in NLP tasks. However, PLMs are prone to encoding stereotypical biases. Although a burgeoning literature has emerged on stereotypical bias mitigation in PLMs, such as work on debiasing gender and racial stereotyping, how such biases manifest and behave internally within PLMs remains largely unknown. Understanding the internal stereotyping mechanisms may allow better assessment of model fairness and guide the development of effective mitigation strategies. In this work, we focus on attention heads, a major component of the Transformer architecture, and propose a bias analysis framework to explore and identify a small set of biased heads that are found to contribute to a PLM's stereotypical bias. We conduct extensive experiments to validate the existence of these biased heads and to better understand how they behave. We investigate gender and racial bias in the English language in two types of Transformer-based PLMs: the encoder-based BERT model and the decoder-based autoregressive GPT model. Overall, the results shed light on understanding the bias behavior in pretrained language models.

papers.title: Computation Mechanism Behind LLM Position Generalization
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) computationally process positional information to enable position generalization, such as tolerance to position perturbations and length generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that LLMs learn a disentanglement of attention logits into positional and semantic components, with a linear correlation of 0.959, and identifies a pattern in intermediate features that enables this effect, providing computational explanations for position generalization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention logits in LLMs can be approximately disentangled into independent positional and semantic components, providing computational explanations for position generalization and insights for controlling these phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Attention logits can be approximated by a 3-axis linear decomposition with high correlation.
Attention logits can be disentangled into a sum of positional relevance and semantic importance components.
A pattern in slow-rotating dimensions of query and key vectors enables this disentanglement, which is learned rather than inherent.
LLMs exhibit robustness to position perturbations in text, feature order, and position encoding, with minimal impact on perplexity and downstream task accuracy.
The disentanglement mechanism explains how length generalization techniques work by keeping attention outputs in-distribution.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily evaluates position robustness involving text order and length generalizations, but real-world language processing tasks often involve more complex positional dependencies.
The extent to which models actively leverage this property during training is unclear.
future_direction: Future research could delve deeper into the specific architectural choices and training data patterns that contribute to this robustness.
Future explanations on how such a mechanism is acquired during training dynamics could greatly enhance the work.
papers.abstract: Most written natural languages are composed of sequences of words and sentences. Similar to humans, large language models (LLMs) exhibit flexibility in handling textual positions - a phenomenon we term position generalization. They can understand texts with position perturbations and generalize to longer texts than those encountered during training with the latest techniques. These phenomena suggest that LLMs handle positions tolerantly, but how LLMs computationally process positional relevance remains largely unexplored. This work connects the linguistic phenomenon with LLMs' computational mechanisms. We show how LLMs enforce certain computational mechanisms for the aforementioned tolerance in position perturbations. Despite the complex design of the self-attention mechanism, this work reveals that LLMs learn a counterintuitive disentanglement of attention logits. Their values show a 0.959 linear correlation with an approximation of the arithmetic sum of positional relevance and semantic importance. Furthermore, we identify a prevalent pattern in intermediate features, which we prove theoretically enables this effect. The pattern, which is different from how randomly initialized parameters would behave, suggests that it is a learned behavior rather than a natural result of the model architecture. Based on these findings, we provide computational explanations and criteria for LLMs' position flexibilities. This work takes a pioneering step in linking position generalization with modern LLMs' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: BiasEdit: Debiasing Stereotyped Language Models via Model Editing
papers.research_question: How to efficiently eliminate stereotypical bias from language models while preserving their language modeling abilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BIAS EDIT, a lightweight model editing method that debiases language models by modifying a small portion of parameters via editor networks, preserving language modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: BIAS EDIT is an efficient model editing method that effectively debiases stereotyped language models with minimal harm to their language modeling and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
BIAS EDIT achieves the best debiasing performance on all bias types compared to baselines, reducing Stereotype Score close to 50%.
Editing upper blocks of language models has less negative impact on language modeling abilities than editing bottom blocks.
BIAS EDIT is robust to gender reversal and semantic generality.
The retention loss Lr is effective in maintaining language modeling capabilities during debiasing.
BIAS EDIT has little to no impact on general capabilities of language models as shown on OpenBookQA, BoolQ, and COPA.
papers.limitation: BIAS EDIT is only evaluated on sentence-level bias modeling examples with gold labels, and lacks evaluation on text generation tasks.
future_direction: Adapting BIAS EDIT to mitigate bias for text generation tasks.
Constructing datasets for bias mitigation in text generation.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have established that language models manifest stereotyped biases. Existing debiasing strategies, such as retraining a model with counterfactual data, representation projection, and prompting often fail to efficiently eliminate bias or directly alter the models' biased internal representations. To address these issues, we propose BiasEdit, an efficient model editing method to remove stereotypical bias from language models through lightweight networks that act as editors to generate parameter updates. BiasEdit employs a debiasing loss guiding editor networks to conduct local edits on partial parameters of a language model for debiasing while preserving the language modeling abilities during editing through a retention loss. Experiments on StereoSet and Crows-Pairs demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of BiasEdit in eliminating bias compared to tangental debiasing baselines and little to no impact on the language models' general capabilities. In addition, we conduct bias tracing to probe bias in various modules and explore bias editing impacts on different components of language models.

papers.title: Attention is not Explanation
papers.research_question: To what extent do attention weights provide meaningful explanations for model predictions in neural NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that standard attention modules in neural NLP models do not provide meaningful explanations for predictions, as attention weights correlate poorly with feature importance measures and can be adversarially manipulated without changing predictions.
papers.conclusion: Standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations for model predictions and should not be treated as though they do.
papers.key_findings:
Learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based and leave-one-out measures of feature importance.
One can construct adversarial attention distributions that are maximally different from the original but yield equivalent predictions.
Randomly permuting attention weights often induces only minimal changes in model output.
Attention weights in simple feedforward (average) encoders show better correlation with feature importance than those in BiLSTM encoders.
For complex encoders like BiLSTM, attention weights are not reliable explanations and should not be treated as such.
papers.limitation:
The Kendall τ correlation measure may be depressed by noise from irrelevant features, potentially affecting the assessment of attention-feature importance correlation.
The study only considered a handful of attention variants and encoder architectures, limiting generalizability.
The work did not consider seq2seq tasks, which are common for attention models.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to seq2seq tasks such as machine translation.
Develop more principled attention mechanisms that provide faithful explanations.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have seen wide adoption in neural NLP models. In addition to improving predictive performance, these are often touted as affording transparency: models equipped with attention provide a distribution over attended-to input units, and this is often presented (at least implicitly) as communicating the relative importance of inputs. However, it is unclear what relationship exists between attention weights and model outputs. In this work, we perform extensive experiments across a variety of NLP tasks that aim to assess the degree to which attention weights provide meaningful `explanations' for predictions. We find that they largely do not. For example, learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based measures of feature importance, and one can identify very different attention distributions that nonetheless yield equivalent predictions. Our findings show that standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations and should not be treated as though they do. Code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/successar/AttentionExplanation.

papers.title: An Analysis for Reasoning Bias of Language Models with Small Initialization
papers.research_question: What is the impact of parameter initialization scale on the training behavior and task preferences of LLMs, and how does small initialization bias models towards reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that small initialization scales bias LLMs towards reasoning tasks, while large scales bias towards memorization, and provides a theoretical explanation based on training dynamics and embedding differentiation.
papers.conclusion: This work enhances understanding of how initialization strategies influence LLM performance on reasoning tasks and offers guidelines for training models to enhance reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller initialization scales lead to faster learning of reasoning tasks compared to memorization tasks.
The embedding space of reasoning tokens becomes more differentiated early in training due to distinct label distributions.
The first attention module in Transformers acts like an average operator and captures reasoning anchors more effectively under small initialization.
Theoretical analysis shows that the gradient flow of embeddings depends on label distributions, leading to differentiated embeddings for reasoning tokens.
Experiments on real language tasks (PrOntoQA vs TinyStories) confirm the reasoning bias with small initialization.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Natural Language Processing by demonstrating exceptional performance across diverse tasks. This study investigates the impact of the parameter initialization scale on the training behavior and task preferences of LLMs. We discover that smaller initialization scales encourage models to favor reasoning tasks, whereas larger initialization scales lead to a preference for memorization tasks. We validate this reasoning bias via real datasets and meticulously designed anchor functions. Further analysis of initial training dynamics suggests that specific model components, particularly the embedding space and self-attention mechanisms, play pivotal roles in shaping these learning biases. We provide a theoretical framework from the perspective of model training dynamics to explain these phenomena. Additionally, experiments on real-world language tasks corroborate our theoretical insights. This work enhances our understanding of how initialization strategies influence LLM performance on reasoning tasks and offers valuable guidelines for training models.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Delving into the Reversal Curse: How Far Can Large Language Models Generalize?
papers.research_question: How does the reversal curse manifest across various tasks, and what are the underlying generalization abilities and problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the reversal curse is more likely a backward recall deficiency, and identifies an inherent 'thinking bias' in LLMs where they preferentially use names to initiate fact recall, which strongly influences their generalization ability based on training data structure.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse is a backward recall deficiency in decoder-only models, and LLMs' inherent thinking bias underscores the critical importance of appropriate training data structure for successful knowledge application and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can generalize to 'B is A' when both A and B are presented in context (e.g., in multiple-choice questions).
Generalization ability is highly correlated with the structure of training documents (works for '[Name] is [Description]' but not the reverse).
LLMs possess an inherent thinking bias: they consistently start fact recall with names provided in the query.
The negative impact of this bias on downstream task performance is hard to mitigate through training alone.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) showcase unprecedented capabilities, they also exhibit certain inherent limitations when facing seemingly trivial tasks. A prime example is the recently debated "reversal curse", which surfaces when models, having been trained on the fact "A is B", struggle to generalize this knowledge to infer that "B is A". In this paper, we examine the manifestation of the reversal curse across various tasks and delve into both the generalization abilities and the problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs. This investigation leads to a series of significant insights: (1) LLMs are able to generalize to "B is A" when both A and B are presented in the context as in the case of a multiple-choice question. (2) This generalization ability is highly correlated to the structure of the fact "A is B" in the training documents. For example, this generalization only applies to biographies structured in "[Name] is [Description]" but not to "[Description] is [Name]". (3) We propose and verify the hypothesis that LLMs possess an inherent bias in fact recalling during knowledge application, which explains and underscores the importance of the document structure to successful learning. (4) The negative impact of this bias on the downstream performance of LLMs can hardly be mitigated through training alone. These findings offer a novel perspective on interpreting LLMs' generalization through their intrinsic mechanisms and provide insights for developing more effective learning methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alibaba/thinking_bias.git.

papers.title: Don’t Forget About Pronouns: Removing Gender Bias in Language Models Without Losing Factual Gender Information
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle and remove gender bias from language model representations while preserving factual gender information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using orthogonal probes to disentangle and filter gender bias from contextual language model representations while preserving factual gender information, showing bias can be reduced without significantly harming language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: It is possible to decrease stereotypical gender bias in language model representations while preserving factual gender information, without significant deterioration of the model's language modeling capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
The method decreases gender bias in profession names (measured by MSE) while preserving factual gender information for gendered nouns.
Filtering bias dimensions only moderately decreases masked language modeling accuracy on general text.
Preserving factual gender dimensions in the filter can improve pronoun prediction accuracy in coreference tasks by removing confounding stereotypical bias.
Probing identifies sparse dimensions in the embedding space that encode bias and factual gender information.
The method works on multiple transformer-based masked language models (BERT and ELECTRA).
papers.limitation:
The method does not remove all gender information, so downstream classifiers could still retrieve gender, making it unsuitable for tasks using gender-biased data.
The method does not fully remove gender bias; some bias remains in the representations.
The linear probe may not capture non-linear encoding of gender signals in the Transformer, and information might be recovered in subsequent layers.
papers.abstract: The representations in large language models contain multiple types of gender information. We focus on two types of such signals in English texts: factual gender information, which is a grammatical or semantic property, and gender bias, which is the correlation between a word and specific gender. We can disentangle the model's embeddings and identify components encoding both types of information with probing. We aim to diminish the stereotypical bias in the representations while preserving the factual gender signal. Our filtering method shows that it is possible to decrease the bias of gender-neutral profession names without significant deterioration of language modeling capabilities. The findings can be applied to language generation to mitigate reliance on stereotypes while preserving gender agreement in coreferences. 1

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Transformers: Insights from The Encoding Specificity Principle
papers.research_question: How do attention layers in transformer-based LLMs implement memory retrieval mechanisms, and are contextual cues represented as keywords?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval, with Q, K, V playing distinct roles analogous to human memory, and that contextual cues are represented as keywords.
papers.conclusion: Attention layers in transformers implement memory retrieval mechanisms guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, with keywords serving as retrieval cues and specific neurons encoding these cues.
papers.key_findings:
Swapping V alone induces hallucinations, indicating V stores content.
Swapping both K and V induces systematic hallucination, showing content-addressable matching and content retrieval.
Swapping K only hinders factual recall, representing retrieval failure.
Consistent, model-specific attention neurons are activated by keywords.
Perturbing keywords at the K matrix impairs memory retrieval.
papers.abstract: While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for large language models (LLMs) remains an evolving field with many unresolved questions, increasing regulatory pressures have spurred interest in its role in ensuring transparency, accountability, and privacy-preserving machine unlearning. Despite recent advances in XAI have provided some insights, the specific role of attention layers in transformer based LLMs remains underexplored. This study investigates the memory mechanisms instantiated by attention layers, drawing on prior research in psychology and computational psycholinguistics that links Transformer attention to cue based retrieval in human memory. In this view, queries encode the retrieval context, keys index candidate memory traces, attention weights quantify cue trace similarity, and values carry the encoded content, jointly enabling the construction of a context representation that precedes and facilitates memory retrieval. Guided by the Encoding Specificity Principle, we hypothesize that the cues used in the initial stage of retrieval are instantiated as keywords. We provide converging evidence for this keywords-as-cues hypothesis. In addition, we isolate neurons within attention layers whose activations selectively encode and facilitate the retrieval of context-defining keywords. Consequently, these keywords can be extracted from identified neurons and further contribute to downstream applications such as unlearning.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
