Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale decoder-only LLMs (7B–9B parameters); whether similar patterns persist in larger models or Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remains an open question.
The neuron pruning strategy is coarse and may disrupt correct generations, limiting overall accuracy gains.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.
Developing more fine-grained or adaptive debiasing methods beyond simple pruning.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks, yet they frequently fail on basic numerical problems, producing incorrect outputs. Inspired by Benford's Law, a statistical pattern in which lower digits occur more frequently as leading digits, we hypothesize that the skewed digit distributions in web-collected corpora may be learned by LLMs during pretraining, leading to biased numerical generation. To investigate the hypothesis, we first examine whether digits frequencies in pretraining corpus (OLMo2) follows Benford's law. We then construct an evaluation benchmark in which the ground-truth digits are uniformly distributed within each of the seven numerical reasoning tasks. Our evaluation results demonstrate that leading open-source LLMs show a consistent pattern of digit bias that resembles Benford's law. Through logit-lens tracing and neuron-level dissection, we identify that this bias arises predominantly from a small subset of highly digit-selective feed-forward network (FFN) neurons in the deeper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that pruning these neurons mitigates imbalanced overgeneration and partially corrects erroneous outputs, providing causal evidence that fine-grained pretraining digit bias can propagate into model behavior. Our findings reveal a fundamental connection between corpus-level statistics and symbolic failure modes in LLMs, offering a new lens for diagnosing and mitigating hallucinations in numerical tasks.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: The Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does symbol grounding emerge in language models, specifically what are the loci and mechanisms driving this emergence?
papers.core_contribution: Symbol grounding emerges in middle-layer computations via aggregate attention heads that retrieve environmental grounds to predict linguistic forms, generalizing across Transformers and state-space models but not LSTMs.
papers.conclusion: Symbol grounding can mechanistically emerge in autoregressive language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations.
Grounding is implemented through an aggregate mechanism where attention heads aggregate environmental ground to support prediction of linguistic forms.
This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models) but not in unidirectional LSTMs.
Grounding cannot be fully explained by co-occurrence statistics.
Causal interventions show that aggregate heads are critical for grounding.
papers.limitation: Full-scale VLMs present additional complications such as large numbers of visual tokens and redundant artifact tokens, making systematic identification and intervention at scale a nontrivial challenge.
future_direction: Investigate how grounding mechanisms interact with other emergent phenomena, such as in-context learning and reasoning.
Scale the analysis to larger models and more naturalistic settings.
papers.abstract: Symbol grounding (Harnad, 1990) describes how symbols such as words acquire their meanings by connecting to real-world sensorimotor experiences. Recent work has shown preliminary evidence that grounding may emerge in (vision-)language models trained at scale without using explicit grounding objectives. Yet, the specific loci of this emergence and the mechanisms that drive it remain largely unexplored. To address this problem, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that systematically traces how symbol grounding arises within the internal computations through mechanistic and causal analysis. Our findings show that grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations and is implemented through the aggregate mechanism, where attention heads aggregate the environmental ground to support the prediction of linguistic forms. This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models), but not in unidirectional LSTMs. Our results provide behavioral and mechanistic evidence that symbol grounding can emerge in language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.

papers.title: Through a Compressed Lens: Investigating The Impact of Quantization on Factual Knowledge Recall
papers.research_question: How does quantization affect factual knowledge recall (FKR) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Quantization typically leads to information loss and degrades factual knowledge recall, especially in smaller models, but BitSandBytes is most effective at preserving FKR and quantization remains a viable compression strategy.
papers.conclusion: Quantization generally leads to information loss and factual knowledge recall degradation, but effects vary by model and technique, and it remains a viable compression strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Quantization typically impairs factual knowledge recall, with more pronounced effects in smaller models within a family.
Models quantized to lower bit precision do not consistently underperform higher-precision versions.
Quantization can occasionally improve factual knowledge recall, possibly due to regularization or noise effects.
BitSandBytes (BITSANDBYTES) quantization best preserves the original model's factual knowledge recall capability.
No observed performance degradation is severe enough to compromise quantization as an effective compression strategy.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are confined to English-language datasets.
Experiments are restricted to Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B due to computational constraints.
The study is limited to post-training quantization techniques and does not include lower-bit quantization (e.g., 1-bit or 2-bit) or weight-activation quantization.
future_direction: Extending experiments to multilingual settings.
Investigating the impact of lower-bit quantization (e.g., 1-bit or 2-bit).
Studying the impact of weight-activation quantization, KV cache compression, or quantization-aware training techniques on factual knowledge recall.
papers.abstract: Quantization methods are widely used to accelerate inference and streamline the deployment of large language models (LLMs). Although quantization's effects on various LLM capabilities have been extensively studied, one critical area remains underexplored: factual knowledge recall (FKR), the process by which LLMs access stored knowledge. To this end, we conduct comprehensive experiments using three common quantization techniques at distinct bit widths, in conjunction with interpretability-driven analyses on two tasks, knowledge memorization and latent multi-hop reasoning. We show that quantization typically results in information loss within LLMs, consequently diminishing their capacity for FKR. This effect is particularly amplified in smaller models within the same architectural families. However, models quantized at reduced bit precision do not consistently exhibit inferior performance and occasionally quantization may even enhance model FKR. We find that BitSandBytes demonstrates highest preservation of the original full-precision model's FKR. Despite variability across models and methods, quantization causes modest performance degradation and remains an effective compression strategy.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: Incremental Processing of Principle B: Mismatches Between Neural Models and Humans
papers.research_question: Do GPT-based autoregressive neural language models use Principle B to restrict their incremental coreference processing like humans? Specifically, does Principle B block the influence of ungrammatical structural positions on pronoun prediction and cataphoric processing?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-based language models do not categorically ignore structural positions blocked by Principle B during incremental coreference processing, unlike humans. This mismatch suggests that certain aspects of human parsing behavior are not directly evidenced in linguistic data and may relate to properties of the training data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive neural models do not uniformly process pronouns like humans; they fail to capture qualitative patterns of incremental coreference processing and underestimate processing costs. Models appear to learn only those aspects of Principle B that have predictable reflexes in training data.
papers.key_findings:
For object pronouns (him) in positions where Principle B blocks co-indexation, all models exhibited a negative Gender Mismatch Effect (GMME), meaning they expected the pronoun to mismatch in gender with the grammatically unavailable antecedent.
For possessive pronouns (his), all models showed positive GMMEs across all structural positions, expecting gender agreement with antecedents.
In cataphoric object pronoun processing, larger models (GPT-J and GPT-3) showed no significant GMME when Principle B blocked coreference, aligning with human behavior, while smaller models (GPT-2 XL and GPT-Neo) showed a positive GMME.
Neural models greatly underestimate the magnitude of processing costs observed in humans, even in cases of qualitative overlap.
Analysis of the training data (the Pile) reveals a surface distribution bias where pronouns are more likely to mismatch in gender with antecedents in positions blocked by Principle B, suggesting models may overfit this pattern.
papers.limitation:
Whether models truly 'interpret' the correct coreference relations is unclear; techniques are limited for assessing if models comprehend meaning in a human-like fashion.
The study relies on stereotypical associations between nouns and pronouns, which does not cleanly map onto the real world (e.g., singular they is not considered).
The investigation is limited to English, due to resource availability and the focus of existing psycholinguistic work, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Future work might consider analyses of the attention mechanisms to dig deeper into what information models are using.
papers.abstract: Despite neural language models qualitatively capturing many human linguistic behaviors, recent work has demonstrated that they underestimate the true processing costs of ungrammatical structures. We extend these more fine-grained comparisons between humans and models by investigating the interaction between Principle B and coreference processing. While humans use Principle B to block certain structural positions from affecting their incremental processing, we find that GPT-based language models are influenced by ungrammatical positions. We conclude by relating the mismatch between neural models and humans to properties of training data and suggest that certain aspects of human processing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.Paper at CoNLL 2022

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Insights into LLM Long-Context Failures: When Transformers Know but Don't Tell
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to utilize information from the middle or end of long contexts, despite encoding that information internally?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies a 'know but don't tell' phenomenon in LLMs, where models encode the position of target information in their hidden representations but often fail to leverage this knowledge to generate accurate responses, especially for information in the middle of long contexts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs capture context information internally but fail to generate correct answers due to positional bias, and delayed extraction of information (requiring more layers) leads to lower generation accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
There is a gap between probing accuracy (internal knowledge) and generation accuracy (output): LLMs can locate information internally but fail to generate correct answers.
Middle-context information requires more transformer layers to be located compared to information at the beginning or end.
The earlier a model locates target information within its layers (shallower peak probing layer), the higher its final generation accuracy for that information.
Positional bias emerges during the model's internal processing, with a noticeable shift in logits at a certain layer depending on the position of the gold information.
papers.limitation: Knowledge of the gold document's location and the ability to cite from it are distinct; the model might know the location but still fail to integrate it into a coherent and accurate answer. The probing comparison does not fully capture the nuanced interactions between the model's internal attention mechanisms and output generation capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit positional bias, struggling to utilize information from the middle or end of long contexts. Our study explores LLMs' long-context reasoning by probing their hidden representations. We find that while LLMs encode the position of target information, they often fail to leverage this in generating accurate responses. This reveals a disconnect between information retrieval and utilization, a "know but don't tell" phenomenon. We further analyze the relationship between extraction time and final accuracy, offering insights into the underlying mechanics of transformer models.

papers.title: UniBias: Unveiling and Mitigating LLM Bias through Internal Attention and FFN Manipulation
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms within LLMs that cause bias, and can we identify and mitigate these biased components to improve in-context learning performance and robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces UniBias, an inference-only method that identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads in LLMs by projecting internal components to vocabulary space and applying three criteria, leading to improved ICL performance and reduced prompt brittleness.
papers.conclusion: UniBias effectively mitigates LLM bias by manipulating internal structures, achieving state-of-the-art ICL performance and enhancing robustness against prompt brittleness.
papers.key_findings:
FFN vectors and attention heads are internal components that contribute to various bias factors like vanilla label bias, recency bias, and selection bias.
UniBias identifies biased components using three criteria: relatedness to label prediction, biased logit distribution, and low variance across samples.
UniBias significantly improves ICL performance across 12 NLP datasets and multiple model sizes (Llama-2 7B/13B, GPT-J, GPT2-XL), outperforming existing calibration methods.
UniBias alleviates prompt brittleness, making model performance more stable under changes in example selection, order, and prompt formatting.
Some biased components are shared across tasks, suggesting the potential for identifying global biased components for cross-task bias mitigation.
papers.limitation: The method relies on grid searching with a small set of labeled training samples.
future_direction: Reduce reliance on labeled samples for grid searching to improve efficiency and applicability.
Identify global biased components that mitigate bias across multiple tasks and diverse prompt settings.
Use identified biased components as sensors for guiding effective prompt generation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various tasks using the in-context learning (ICL) paradigm. However, their effectiveness is often compromised by inherent bias, leading to prompt brittleness, i.e., sensitivity to design settings such as example selection, order, and prompt formatting. Previous studies have addressed LLM bias through external adjustment of model outputs, but the internal mechanisms that lead to such bias remain unexplored. Our work delves into these mechanisms, particularly investigating how feedforward neural networks (FFNs) and attention heads result in the bias of LLMs. By Interpreting the contribution of individual FFN vectors and attention heads, we identify the biased LLM components that skew LLMs' prediction toward specific labels. To mitigate these biases, we introduce UniBias, an inference-only method that effectively identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads. Extensive experiments across 12 NLP datasets demonstrate that UniBias significantly enhances ICL performance and alleviates prompt brittleness of LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding through Numerical Attributes in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally integrate multiple numerical attributes of a single entity? How does irrelevant numerical context perturb these representations and their downstream outputs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode numerical attributes in shared linear subspaces, amplify real-world correlations, and are vulnerable to irrelevant numerical context, with smaller models being more susceptible.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal vulnerabilities in LLM decision-making under multi-attribute entanglement and lay groundwork for fairer, representation-aware control in numerically-sensitive applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode multiple numerical attributes of an entity in overlapping internal subspaces.
Internal correlations between attributes can exceed the natural correlations observed in the data.
Asymmetric interference patterns exist where certain dominant attributes exert disproportionate influence over others in the representation.
Irrelevant numerical context in prompts perturbs internal representations and degrades output reliability, especially in smaller models.
Larger models are more robust to such perturbations, likely due to more complex computations.
papers.limitation:
The method does not scale to multiple concurrent confounders and is limited by a single-confounder assumption.
The study focused only on fact-retrieval tasks and did not explore arithmetic reasoning under in-context learning.
No single subspace was identified that uniformly represents arbitrary numerical features.
future_direction: Employ multivariate causal inference or factor-analytic techniques to disentangle complex attribute relationships.
Conduct a broader study including generative and multi-step arithmetic reasoning scenarios.
papers.abstract: Although behavioral studies have documented numerical reasoning errors in large language models (LLMs), the underlying representational mechanisms remain unclear. We hypothesize that numerical attributes occupy shared latent subspaces and investigate two questions:(1) How do LLMs internally integrate multiple numerical attributes of a single entity? (2)How does irrelevant numerical context perturb these representations and their downstream outputs? To address these questions, we combine linear probing with partial correlation analysis and prompt-based vulnerability tests across models of varying sizes. Our results show that LLMs encode real-world numerical correlations but tend to systematically amplify them. Moreover, irrelevant context induces consistent shifts in magnitude representations, with downstream effects that vary by model size. These findings reveal a vulnerability in LLM decision-making and lay the groundwork for fairer, representation-aware control under multi-attribute entanglement.

papers.title: Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon (U-shaped performance curve)? The paper investigates whether this behavior emerges from adaptations to short-term and long-term information retrieval demands during training.
papers.core_contribution: The lost-in-the-middle behavior in LLMs emerges from joint optimization on short-term and long-term information retrieval demands, and is influenced by architectural biases (autoregressive design) and attention sinks.
papers.conclusion: The lost-in-the-middle phenomenon is an emergent property from information retrieval demands, influenced by model architecture and attention dynamics, rather than a simple flaw.
papers.key_findings:
Training on free recall (long-term demand) yields primacy, on running span (short-term demand) yields recency, and joint training yields the U-shaped lost-in-the-middle curve.
Primacy effect arises from uniform long-term demand and is shaped by autoregressive architecture (causal masking), as shown by comparison with T5.
Recency effect directly aligns with the shape of short-term demand in training data.
Attention sinks support primacy under long-term memory demand; ablating them impairs free recall but not running span.
The effects generalize to masked sequence completion tasks, which more closely resemble next-token prediction.
future_direction: Uncovering connections between artificial and biological systems in memory phenomena.
papers.abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) often degrades when crucial information is in the middle of a long context, a "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon that mirrors the primacy and recency effects in human memory. We propose that this behavior is not simply a flaw indicative of information loss but an adaptation to different information retrieval demands during pre-training: some tasks require uniform recall across the entire input (a long-term memory demand), while others prioritize the most recent information (a short-term memory demand). Consistent with this view, we show that this U-shaped performance curve emerges when LLMs (GPT-2 and Llama variants) are trained from scratch on two simple human memory paradigms simulating long-term and short-term memory demands. Our analysis reveals that while the recency effect directly aligns with short-term memory demand in the training data, the primacy effect is induced by the uniform long-term memory demand and is additionally influenced by the model's autoregressive properties and the formation of attention sinks. Our main findings from simple human memory paradigms also generalize to a sequence completion task, which more closely resembles the next-token prediction process in LLM pre-training. Together, our findings reveal how information retrieval demands, model architecture, and structural attention dynamics during model training can jointly produce positional bias observed in LLMs.

papers.title: A Glitch in the Matrix? Locating and Detecting Language Model Grounding with Fakepedia
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to ground answers in contextual information that contradicts their parametric knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset, and MGCT, a causal mediation analysis method, to study grounding in LLMs, finding that grounding is a distributed process and that computational patterns can predict grounding behavior.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that grounding is a distributed process, ungrounded responses involve factual recall in MLPs, and grounding can be predicted from computation patterns, contributing to a coherent narrative of grounding and factual recall mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding, contrary to factual recall, is a distributed process without clear localization.
The activity of a few MLPs differs significantly between grounded and ungrounded modes.
Computational patterns can predict whether a model is grounded with 92.8% accuracy.
Models exhibit diverse grounding behaviors; e.g., Mistral-7B is highly compliant while GPT-4 Turbo strongly prefers parametric knowledge.
Not grounding involves activating factual recall processes in the MLPs of the final subject token.
papers.limitation:
Descriptive analysis may be influenced by the choice of prompting strategy.
Mediation setup requires the object token to be the last token; different behaviors might emerge in other setups.
Automatic detection model may not generalize outside the experimental domain.
Does not distinguish between plausible and absurd counterfactual facts.
Dataset generation could be improved with interaction flows based on other language models as critics.
future_direction: Explore relationship between prompting strategy and grounding frequency.
Study grounding behavior in different experimental setups.
Investigate how grounding varies with the likelihood of counterfactual facts.
Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: How Pre-trained Language Models Capture Factual Knowledge? A Causal-Inspired Analysis
papers.research_question: Which word-level associations (knowledge-dependent, positionally close, highly co-occurred) do Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) depend on to capture factual knowledge, and is this dependence effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained language models capture factual knowledge more by relying on positionally close and highly co-occurred words than knowledge-dependent words, and that this dependence is less effective for factual knowledge capture.
papers.conclusion: PLMs capture factual knowledge ineffectively because they rely more on positionally close and highly co-occurred associations rather than knowledge-dependent associations.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs depend more on positionally close and highly co-occurred associations than the knowledge-dependent association to capture factual knowledge.
Depending on the knowledge-dependent association is more effective for factual knowledge capture than positional close and highly co-occurred associations.
PLMs capture factual knowledge ineffectively because they depend more on ineffective associations.
Dependence on positionally close words leads to overfitting on pre-training samples and poor generalization to unseen queries.
The proposed causal-inspired method can quantify word-level dependence in mask language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recently, there has been a trend to investigate the factual knowledge captured by Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs). Many works show the PLMs' ability to fill in the missing factual words in cloze-style prompts such as "Dante was born in [MASK]." However, it is still a mystery how PLMs generate the results correctly: relying on effective clues or shortcut patterns? We try to answer this question by a causal-inspired analysis that quantitatively measures and evaluates the word-level patterns that PLMs depend on to generate the missing words. We check the words that have three typical associations with the missing words: knowledge-dependent, positionally close, and highly co-occurred. Our analysis shows: (1) PLMs generate the missing factual words more by the positionally close and highly co-occurred words than the knowledge-dependent words; (2) the dependence on the knowledge-dependent words is more effective than the positionally close and highly co-occurred words. Accordingly, we conclude that the PLMs capture the factual knowledge ineffectively because of depending on the inadequate associations.

papers.title: CBEval: A framework for evaluating and interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive biases manifest in large language models, and can they be interpreted using a framework based on Shapley value analysis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a framework (CBE VAL) using Shapley value analysis to interpret and understand a host of cognitive biases in frontier LLMs, introducing round number bias and the concept of a cognitive bias barrier.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully interprets cognitive shortcomings in LLMs, revealing biases that arise from training heuristics, model characteristics like in-context learning, and the training data itself, similar to human cognitive biases.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit several cognitive biases including framing effect, anchoring effect, representativeness heuristic, priming effect, and a newly identified round number bias.
Shapley value analysis can be used to construct influence graphs that identify the words and phrases most responsible for the manifested biases.
A cognitive bias barrier is identified, representing the point at which an LLM understands a lower loss percentage corresponds to a higher profit percentage.
Models like GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini show differences in their cognitive bias barriers, indicating varying levels of robustness in decision-making.
Anchoring and priming effects, while similar, are hypothesized to rely on different model mechanisms: anchoring on the attention mechanism and priming on associative mappings in MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on output probability distributions; model responses can change due to token noise rather than actual reasoning.
Different system prompts produce slightly different probability distributions, though the main findings hold.
For some models (Mistral Large, Claude, Google Gemini), the API does not provide token probability scores, limiting analysis to subjective evaluation.
The experimentation was conducted prior to the release of the GPT-o1 model, so it is not included.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in Large Language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced their reasoning capabilities. Despite improved performance on benchmarks, LLMs exhibit notable gaps in their cognitive processes. Additionally, as reflections of human-generated data, these models have the potential to inherit cognitive biases, raising concerns about their reasoning and decision making capabilities. In this paper we present a framework to interpret, understand and provide insights into a host of cognitive biases in LLMs. Conducting our research on frontier language models we're able to elucidate reasoning limitations and biases, and provide reasoning behind these biases by constructing influence graphs that identify phrases and words most responsible for biases manifested in LLMs. We further investigate biases such as round number bias and cognitive bias barrier revealed when noting framing effect in language models.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Interpreting Bias in Large Language Models: A Feature-Based Approach
papers.research_question: How do biases propagate in large language models, and how can they be interpreted and mitigated using a feature-based approach?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-based method for analyzing and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, identifying the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation, and demonstrating targeted debiasing using counterfactual datasets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel feature-based approach for interpreting and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, showing that targeted interventions can reduce bias and providing insights into bias mechanisms for future ethical AI development.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias in LLMs originates in early layers, primarily through MLPs, as shown by activation patching experiments.
Attention heads copy bias from profession tokens to final token positions, propagating bias through the network, validated via attribution patching.
Targeted debiasing by fine-tuning identified components (MLPs or attention heads) can reduce bias, but effectiveness varies across models and may be limited by dataset size.
The feature-based approach is extensible to other forms of gender bias, such as stereotypes in household duties, by mapping features to model components.
Patching MLP outputs or attention heads can reverse biased logit orders without losing profession information in generated text, indicating selective intervention.
papers.limitation:
Potential compensation phenomenon where other components take over after patching, which may affect analysis.
Restricted to English language bias only, limiting generalizability.
The approach may require case-by-case tweaking, which is not scalable for multiple biases.
future_direction: Exploring bias interactions in multilingual settings
Examining the impact of debiasing across languages from a white-box perspective
Investigating applicability to other areas like AI security and alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Mistral and LLaMA have showcased remarkable performance across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Despite their success, these models inherit social biases from the diverse datasets on which they are trained. This paper investigates the propagation of biases within LLMs through a novel feature-based analytical approach. Drawing inspiration from causal mediation analysis, we hypothesize the evolution of bias-related features and validate them using interpretability techniques like activation and attribution patching. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce and empirically validate a feature-based method for bias analysis in LLMs, applied to LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 with templates from a professions dataset. (2) We extend our method to another form of gender bias, demonstrating its generalizability. (3) We differentiate the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation and implement targeted debiasing using a counterfactual dataset. Our findings reveal the complex nature of bias in LLMs and emphasize the necessity for tailored debiasing strategies, offering a deeper understanding of bias mechanisms and pathways for effective mitigation.

papers.title: Deconstructing Positional Information: From Attention Logits to Training Biases
papers.research_question: How do different positional encoding schemes (additive vs. multiplicative) mediate the interaction between token content and position, and what causes the performance paradox and single-head deposit pattern in RoPE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified Toeplitz-matrix framework to analyze positional encodings, discovers the single-head deposit pattern in RoPE, and provides a theoretical explanation showing this pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE's multiplicative structure.
papers.conclusion: The Toeplitz framework provides a powerful lens for understanding positional encodings, and the deposit pattern explains RoPE's performance paradox. Controlled mixing of positional signals is a promising strategy for achieving robust, distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE's multiplicative structure enables superior performance on tasks requiring content-position coupling but leads to a single-head deposit pattern where positional information is concentrated in one early-layer head.
Additive positional encodings (Absolute, T5, ALiBi) do not exhibit the deposit pattern and show different learning dynamics.
The deposit pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE, caused by exponential amplification of gradient signals during training, leading to extreme specialization.
Hybrid architectures like Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) can mitigate the deposit pattern and improve robustness by mixing positional signals.
RoPE's strong inductive bias suppresses the formation of latent positional representations observed in models with additive or no PE.
papers.limitation:
The connection between the deposit pattern and RoPE's known struggles with length extrapolation requires direct empirical validation.
Future work should probe the limits of these positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks such as sequence reversal or Dyck language recognition.
future_direction: Direct empirical validation of the link between the deposit pattern and length extrapolation.
Testing positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks.
More complex controlled analysis of positional mechanisms in transformers.
papers.abstract: Positional encodings enable Transformers to incorporate sequential information, yet their theoretical understanding remains limited to two properties: distance attenuation and translation invariance. Because natural language lacks purely positional data, the interplay between positional and semantic information is still underexplored. We address this gap by deconstructing the attention-logit computation and providing a structured analysis of positional encodings, categorizing them into additive and multiplicative forms. The differing properties of these forms lead to distinct mechanisms for capturing positional information. To probe this difference, we design a synthetic task that explicitly requires strong integration of positional and semantic cues. As predicted, multiplicative encodings achieve a clear performance advantage on this task. Moreover, our evaluation reveals a hidden training bias: an information aggregation effect in shallow layers that we term the single-head deposit pattern. Through ablation studies and theoretical analysis, we proved that this phenomenon is inherent in multiplicative encodings. These findings deepen the understanding of positional encodings and call for further study of their training dynamics.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations in Base 10
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent numbers? Specifically, do they use digit-wise representations in base 10 rather than a linear value space?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally represent numbers using individual circular representations per-digit in base 10, which explains their error patterns on numerical tasks.
papers.conclusion: Circular digit-wise probes can effectively extract number representations in base 10, and editing these representations can alter model generation, suggesting digit-wise representations are used for arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
LLM errors on numerical tasks are often scattered across the digits of the answer rather than normally distributed around its numeric value.
Probes can accurately recover digit values in base 10 from hidden representations, but not the whole number value directly.
Causal interventions on digit representations can modify the number accordingly, confirming the causal significance of digit-wise representations.
The digit-wise representation is base-10 specific, with high accuracy for base 10 probes compared to other bases.
This representation holds across models with different tokenization schemes, such as Llama 3 8B and Mistral 7B.
papers.limitation:
The study does not conclusively show that digit-wise representation is the only representation of numeracy in LLMs; there may be superposition of multiple redundant representations.
The focus is exclusively on natural numbers, leaving fractions and other numeric values for future work.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to fractions and other numeric values beyond natural numbers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently make errors when handling even simple numerical problems, such as comparing two small numbers. A natural hypothesis is that these errors stem from how LLMs represent numbers, and specifically, whether their representations of numbers capture their numeric values. We tackle this question from the observation that LLM errors on numerical tasks are often distributed across the digits of the answer rather than normally around its numeric value. Through a series of probing experiments and causal interventions, we show that LLMs internally represent numbers with individual circular representations per-digit in base 10. This digit-wise representation, as opposed to a value representation, sheds light on the error patterns of models on tasks involving numerical reasoning and could serve as a basis for future studies on analyzing numerical mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Semantic and Structural Analysis of Implicit Biases in Large Language Models: An Interpretable Approach
papers.research_question: How to identify and explain implicit stereotypes in large language models using an interpretable bias detection method?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable bias detection method for large language models that integrates nested semantic representation with attention perturbation to identify hidden social biases in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The interpretable detection method effectively identifies implicit biases in LLMs, improving detection accuracy and semantic consistency, and provides a foundation for bias intervention and ethical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves higher bias detection accuracy (84.7%), semantic consistency (91.2%), and lower contextual sensitivity (8.5) compared to baselines.
It demonstrates strong generalization across multiple stereotype dimensions, with higher accuracy for gender and profession than for religion and race.
Higher semantic similarity between texts leads to more consistent bias judgments, reducing conflict rates.
Attention perturbation analysis reveals the model's sensitivity to social attribute terms, helping uncover bias pathways.
The method provides interpretable insights into how implicit stereotypes are formed in language models.
papers.limitation: Performance declines on more complex, culturally embedded biases such as religion and race due to their subtlety and ambiguity.
future_direction: Expand the method's adaptability to cross-cultural and multilingual contexts.
Integrate external knowledge bases and user feedback signals for more flexible bias detection.
Embed interpretability mechanisms into model interaction interfaces for user perception and response.
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the issue of implicit stereotypes that may arise during the generation process of large language models. It proposes an interpretable bias detection method aimed at identifying hidden social biases in model outputs, especially those semantic tendencies that are not easily captured through explicit linguistic features. The method combines nested semantic representation with a contextual contrast mechanism. It extracts latent bias features from the vector space structure of model outputs. Using attention weight perturbation, it analyzes the model's sensitivity to specific social attribute terms, thereby revealing the semantic pathways through which bias is formed. To validate the effectiveness of the method, this study uses the StereoSet dataset, which covers multiple stereotype dimensions including gender, profession, religion, and race. The evaluation focuses on several key metrics, such as bias detection accuracy, semantic consistency, and contextual sensitivity. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves strong detection performance across various dimensions. It can accurately identify bias differences between semantically similar texts while maintaining high semantic alignment and output stability. The method also demonstrates high interpretability in its structural design. It helps uncover the internal bias association mechanisms within language models. This provides a more transparent and reliable technical foundation for bias detection. The approach is suitable for real-world applications where high trustworthiness of generated content is required.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
papers.research_question: Does attention provide a faithful explanation for model decisions by identifying important input components?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not reliably interpretable as importance indicators; they are only noisy predictors of input components' importance to the model.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not an optimal method of identifying which attended elements are responsible for an output; as an importance ranking, it fails to explain model decisions.
papers.key_findings:
The highest attention weight often has a larger impact than a random weight, but there are many cases where the impact is similar.
Attention weights often fail to identify the minimal set of representations that are important for the model's decision.
Gradient-based rankings of attention weights often predict their effects better than their magnitudes.
The scope of contextualization (e.g., RNN vs. convolutional encoders) affects how well attention indicates importance.
In encoderless models, attention magnitudes are more helpful, but still not optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on text classification, which may not generalize to tasks with larger output spaces (e.g., language modeling).
Reliance on argmax decision flips as a measure of importance, which might be too coarse.
Only evaluated on specific attention functions (additive attention) and final layers; other variants and lower layers might behave differently.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other tasks and models with larger output spaces.
Develop better, more informative importance rankings.
Align models with human feedback for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have recently boosted performance on a range of NLP tasks. Because attention layers explicitly weight input components' representations, it is also often assumed that attention can be used to identify information that models found important (e.g., specific contextualized word tokens). We test whether that assumption holds by manipulating attention weights in already-trained text classification models and analyzing the resulting differences in their predictions. While we observe some ways in which higher attention weights correlate with greater impact on model predictions, we also find many ways in which this does not hold, i.e., where gradient-based rankings of attention weights better predict their effects than their magnitudes. We conclude that while attention noisily predicts input components' overall importance to a model, it is by no means a fail-safe indicator. 1

papers.title: Identifying and Mitigating Social Bias Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate social biases in language models while preserving individual commonsense knowledge and factual integrity?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a fine-grained debiasing framework (FAST) that localizes and mitigates social bias knowledge in language models while preserving commonsense knowledge, and introduces the BiaScope benchmark for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed fine-grained debiasing framework effectively mitigates social biases while preserving factual knowledge, demonstrating the potential of localized interventions for fairness in language models.
papers.key_findings:
FAST achieves superior debiasing performance on StereoSet, Crows-Pairs, and BiaScope compared to existing methods.
FAST retains commonsense knowledge better than group-invariant debiasing methods, as measured by the Retention Score.
Bias knowledge is localized in specific layers (e.g., the last layer of BERT), and intervening at these layers is most effective.
FAST scales to larger models like GPT2-XL, GPT-Neo-2.7b, and Llama-2-7b, showing consistent debiasing performance.
FAST maintains language modeling capability on downstream GLUE tasks, indicating minimal impact on general performance.
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human-relevant social bias knowledge to process, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive to collect.
Social bias in open language generation or dialogue is not addressed.
Debiasing performance on larger models is less pronounced compared to smaller models.
future_direction: Integrate automated social bias detection methods to enhance construction of biased knowledge base.
Expand the fairness edit method to open language generation or dialogue scenarios.
Improve debiasing performance on larger models with more intricate knowledge.
papers.abstract: Generating fair and accurate predictions plays a pivotal role in deploying large language models (LLMs) in the real world. However, existing debiasing methods inevitably generate unfair or incorrect predictions as they are designed and evaluated to achieve parity across different social groups but leave aside individual commonsense facts, resulting in modified knowledge that elicits unreasonable or undesired predictions. In this paper, we first establish a new bias mitigation benchmark, BiaScope, which systematically assesses performance by leveraging newly constructed datasets and metrics on knowledge retention and generalization. Then, we propose a novel debiasing approach, Fairness Stamp (FAST), which enables fine-grained calibration of individual social biases. FAST identifies the decisive layer responsible for storing social biases and then calibrates its outputs by integrating a small modular network, considering both bias mitigation and knowledge-preserving demands. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that FAST surpasses state-of-the-art baselines with superior debiasing performance while not compromising the overall model capability for knowledge retention and downstream predictions. This highlights the potential of fine-grained debiasing strategies to achieve fairness in LLMs.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models.
